analysis.one_liner: Gives dollar-for-dollar federal tax credits, up to $10 billion a year, for donations to private school scholarship and job training funds.
analysis.headline: Sens. Ted Cruz and five Republican cosponsors sent the bill to the Senate Finance Committee in January 2023, where it sat for two years without a markup, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let individuals and corporations claim a federal tax credit equal to every dollar they donate to organizations that give out private K-12 school scholarships or fund job training and apprenticeships. Total credits would be capped at $10 billion a year, split evenly between school scholarships and workforce training. It would also bar states from disfavoring religious or private education providers and forbid any federal control over private, religious, or home education providers.
analysis.who_benefits: Students who receive scholarships for private K-12 tuition or job training; the private and religious schools they attend; workforce training organizations, community colleges, and apprenticeship programs; and the donors and corporations whose tax bills are reduced dollar-for-dollar by their contributions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Private schools, donors, and training programs

how_it_helps.text: Individuals get a federal tax credit equal to the full amount of a cash contribution, capped at 10% of adjusted gross income, with up to five years to carry forward unused credit; corporations get the same full credit capped at 5% of taxable income.

Total credits are capped at $10 billion per calendar year, with $5 billion for scholarship-granting organizations and $5 billion for workforce training organizations such as community colleges, apprenticeship programs, and organizations run by collective bargaining groups.

Scholarship money is weighted toward need: of the school-scholarship funds not already reserved for a state's prior-year use, 80% is allocated based on the number of children aged 5-17 from families below the poverty line.
Scholarships are not treated as income to the student or parents and cannot be counted against eligibility for any other federal program.

States and the federal portal may not disfavor education providers based on religious character, and nothing in the bill authorizes federal control over private, religious, or home education providers.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally, through up to $10 billion a year in forgone federal revenue; the money is diverted from the general treasury to education funds chosen by individual donors and corporations.

drawbacks.text: A dollar-for-dollar credit means contributors give at no net cost to themselves — they redirect tax they would owe anyway. That channel is most useful to higher-income individuals (who owe enough tax to use credits up to 10% of income) and corporations, and it lets private parties direct where federal revenue goes.
The bill strips federal revenue of up to $10 billion a year that would otherwise flow to the treasury, without a direct offsetting funding increase for public schools.

The bill bars participating states from excluding or disadvantaging providers based on religious character and forbids any federal control over private, religious, or home education providers, so scholarship dollars could pay tuition at private schools not subject to public accountability rules.

Families already paying private school tuition are positioned to capture scholarships, since an eligible scholarship-granting organization must serve students at more than one education provider but need not restrict awards to students leaving public school.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill does include equity features — 80% of the unreserved scholarship allocation is weighted to children in poverty, and half the money goes to workforce training that community colleges and apprenticeship programs could use. But its core mechanism is a dollar-for-dollar credit that lets donors and corporations redirect tax payments they would owe anyway into funds of their choosing, with the bill explicitly shielding religious and private providers from federal oversight. The public benefit depends entirely on private donors choosing to fund low-income scholarships; the $10 billion annual revenue cost and the weakened accountability are guaranteed.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on January 24, 2023, and the committee never took it up, so it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Ted Cruz introduced the bill on January 24, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day.
Five Republican senators cosponsored the bill.
The action history shows no markup, no committee vote, no floor action, and no further activity of any kind after the referral, through the end of the 118th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the federal treasury kept up to $10 billion a year it would otherwise have forgone, and no federal tax-credit channel to private schools was created. Supporters of private school scholarships, would-be donors, and scholarship organizations gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The treasury and public school funding

for.name: Sen. Ted Cruz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on January 24, 2023.

against.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired took no action on the bill after referral — no markup, no vote, and no floor scheduling in two years.

sides.party_line_note: All sponsorship came from Republicans — the sponsor and 5 of 49 Senate Republican cosponsors — with no recorded Democratic support, and the Democratic-chaired Finance Committee never brought it up; no vote was ever taken.

industries.note: The bill would make 501(c)(3) scholarship-granting organizations the permanent channel for $5 billion a year in federal tax credits, requiring them to pass at least 90% of contributions to scholarships. They would administer public money with donor-chosen direction and limited federal oversight.

Scholarship dollars could pay tuition at private and religious schools, and the bill bars states from disfavoring providers on religious grounds while forbidding federal control over them. Some families would get tuition help, paid for by federal revenue forgone.

A dollar-for-dollar credit lets those who owe substantial tax redirect up to 10% of income (individuals) or 5% of taxable income (corporations) from the treasury to education funds of their choosing at zero net cost. The credit would be worth little to households with small tax bills.

The bill makes no direct cut to public school funding, but it would divert up to $10 billion a year of federal revenue to a private-school channel and create competition for students, without any compensating increase in public education funding.

industries.industry: Workforce training providers, community colleges, and apprenticeship programs
industries.note: Half the $10 billion annual cap is reserved for contributions to eligible workforce training organizations, including community colleges, apprenticeship programs, and union-run training. This portion would fund education and training directly for students and workers.
